## Port Eynon to Rhossili Circular: A Jekyll and Hyde hike

![Rhossili](../../images/rhossili%202.jpg)

This almost 14-mile circular walk (13.89 miles in five hours and 42 minutes) follows the stunning coastal path from Port Eynon to Rhossili and Worms Head, back through a rather unconventional tour of the Welsh countryside. I hesitated on whether to refer to this as a walk or a hike, my threshold admittedly high, but I would put this somewhere in the middle of the two, likely towards the hike end. With an elevation gain of 1775 feet, there are certainly enough coastal hills to satisfy a walker who likes to feel a little out of breath. As I will soon indulge, this walk took me a little longer than I first anticipated, largely because the route I was following (which I found on the brilliant app All Trails), took me through an almost traumatising assault of nature through dozens of overgrown “paths” and fields of maize towering well above my head. 

I left Port Eynon before nine, and the first leg of the journey took me through familiar territory. The coast path which runs the stretch between the two beaches is beautiful, with hidden coves dotted along the shore, and only a few diversions from the edge of the cliff. When the coast path eventually exhausts itself, you pass through a couple of fields with the beautiful silhouette of Worms Head before you, eventually to verge onto the concrete walkway that leads you up to the Rhossili car park, National Trust shop and cute cafes. I have been to Rhossili many times, so did not stop here for long, buoyed by exceeding the hallway point on the hike. I will say that this is a lovely point to stop at for a good view of Rhossili, a beautiful, sprawling beach which in person seems astonishingly large. There is a small gallery past the church with local paintings and jewellery, as well as an award-winning café, which I returned to the next day for a drink and some houmous. Towards Worms Head, you can find Rhossili Sunflowers, where I have never gone to pick the flowers, but several times to photograph them. It’s busier than the preceding sections by far. In fact, on my walk from Port Eynon across the coast path, until I reached within twenty minutes of Worms Head, I only met one other person (to whom I said a perfunctory good morning and moved on). I was alone on this walk, utterly alone for most of it, in a feeling of such abject remoteness that sometimes in dips and valleys there was a vacuum of noise, where even the sound of the ocean was smothered by the angles of the cliffs. 

![En Route](../../images/rhossili%203.jpg)

Past Rhossili, I started the second part of my journey, the Hyde to the Jekyll of the coastal path. I had been warned that the hike would be ‘hard’, but once again, I struggled to classify between a walk and a hike (not because I am a particularly fit or adventurous person, although I am attempting to rectify this, but because I consider a hike to be something which pushes me to my complete limits, which, granted this walk did do, if mentally rather than physically), and thought that the difficulty of the hills were exaggerated. I hit peak elevation just past the Rhossili carpark, where I had to climb up to the cliffs overlooking the village and beach, fight through ferns and bracken on barely visible paths until I eventually made it back down to what first appeared to be a public pathway and later turned out to definitely be someone’s private property. This first diversion, where I had to abandon the route I was given as the path was so overgrown with brambles that I could not make it through, definitely should have been taken as an omen for things to come. After climbing over someone’s electric gated fence (with much grace and decorum) and readjusting my path to divert from the brambles, I continued with optimism.

The worst was yet to come. The route back was almost completely impassible. I survived (barely) with just a few scratches from brambles on my legs and arms, but with a whole lot of mental turmoil. I am pretty sure that I unwillingly trespassed multiple times, spending at least two hours collectively in my second-half circular fighting through maize fields with no visibility of where I was, overgrown paths which clearly were once usable from the gates conspicuously placed in the middle, finding sheep jaws and calves under the watchful eyes of their mothers. In the peak of drought, I even managed to get stuck in a bog! This brought my first half from an enjoyable, visually stunning stroll to a battle through what felt like the deepest depths of the jungle, where above all else I needed a panga or machete. When I did eventually return to Port Eynon, having run through nearly six hours of music, two sandwiches and a bottle of water, I was met with an aggressive blister and a billion burrs stuck to my trousers (which in my fear of ticks had been tucked into my long yellow socks). The moment it was over, however, despite the grumbling and moaning, I wanted to go right back and start it all again.
